description_full: Kimco Realty is a real estate investment trust (REIT) and leading owner and operator of high-quality, open-air, grocery-anchored shopping centers and mixed-use properties in the United States. The company's portfolio is strategically concentrated in the first-ring suburbs of the top major metropolitan markets, including high-barrier-to-entry coastal markets and Sun Belt cities. Its tenant mix is focused on essential, necessity-based goods and services that drive multiple shopping trips per week. The company has specialized in shopping center ownership, management, acquisitions, and value-enhancing redevelopment activities for more than 65 years. With a proven commitment to corporate responsibility, Kimco Realty is a recognized industry leader in this area. As of September 30, 2026, the company owned interests in 561 U.S. shopping centers and mixed-use assets comprising 99 million square feet of gross leasable space. Kimco Realty Corporation was incorporated in 1958 in Maryland and is based in Jericho, New York.

financial_summary: Kimco Realty Corporation (HC) is a large-cap real estate business with a $17.0B market cap on $2.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 51 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.92× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.4× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.2% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 36% operating margin runs 13pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.81x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 1.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 15% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 18% and a beta of 0.82, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.18 vs 5y 0.79), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $114.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 61% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 83% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 2% below its DCF fair value of $26.04, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 55%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $19.19 to $36.26 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-0%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 21 covering analysts target $26.18 on average, 3% above the price.
The price implies 2.1% annual cash-flow growth, 4pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.37).
It converts 51% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.92x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 51%.
ROE of 6% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.4x net debt to EBITDA ($211.6M of cash against $7.7B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.32 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.4% over 3 years, 15.1% over 5 years and 6.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 13.7% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 65, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 14.1% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.2%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 4.9% a year to shareholders (0.7% in buybacks and 4.4% in dividends).
The share count has grown 1.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 34 consecutive years, raising it 13.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 710 employees, each generates about $3.0M of revenue, 1.3x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 6.5% a year.
That works out to $1.6M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.5M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
